text: Dangerously in Love is the debut solo studio album by American singer-songwriter Beyoncé, released on June 20, 2003, by Columbia Records and Music World Entertainment. The album features guest appearances from Jay-Z, Missy Elliott, Sean Paul, Big Boi of Outkast, Sleepy Brown, and Luther Vandross, with international editions including vocals from Vanness Wu and IAM. Musically, it combines uptempo tracks and ballads primarily in the R&B genre, incorporating elements of soul, hip-hop, and Arabic music. Recording sessions took place from March 2002 to March 2003 at various studios during Destiny's Child's hiatus, with Beyoncé serving as executive producer, co-writing most songs, selecting which tracks to produce, and contributing to mixing and mastering. Although she did not create beats, she developed melodies and shared ideas with producers. The album's title comes from a track originally on Destiny's Child's 2001 album Survivor, which was re-recorded by Beyoncé and retitled "Dangerously in Love 2" after being deemed too sophisticated for the original release. Lyrically, love is the central theme, with several tracks suggesting a romantic relationship with Jay-Z, including "Signs," which references his zodiac sign, and other songs that explore romance, honesty, and the emotional aspects of love, including breakups and a woman's desire for control. The album also includes a hidden track, "Daddy," a tribute to her father Mathew Knowles, which she later included as a closing track despite initially considering it immature. The album cover was photographed by Markus Klinko, featuring Beyoncé in a diamond-themed outfit, with the top and jeans provided by Tina Knowles and Klinko, respectively, and the image edited to conceal her breasts. Beyoncé faced challenges convincing Columbia Records to release the album, with executives initially doubting its success, and the release date was delayed from October 2002 to May 2003, then to June 2003, to avoid competition with Kelly Rowland's "Dilemma." Despite these delays, the album debuted at number one on the US Billboard 200 with 317,000 copies sold in its first week and received mixed reviews from critics. It won five Grammy Awards at the 46th Annual Grammy Awards in 2004, including Best Contemporary R&B Album, tying Beyoncé with Lauryn Hill, Alicia Keys, and Norah Jones for the most Grammy Awards won by a woman at a single ceremony. The album has been certified septuple platinum by the RIAA and has sold over 11 million copies worldwide as of 2011, making it one of the best-selling albums of the 21st century. It produced four singles: "Crazy in Love," which spent eight consecutive weeks at number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 and won two Grammy Awards; "Baby Boy," which outlasted "Crazy in Love" by one week at the top; "Me, Myself and I," which peaked at number four on the Hot 100; and "Naughty Girl," which reached number three on the Hot 100 and the top ten in several countries. The final single was a cover of "The Closer I Get to You" by Beyoncé and Luther Vandross. Beyoncé promoted the album through live performances, including the Dangerously in Love Tour (2003) and the Verizon Ladies First Tour (2004), co-headlined with Alicia Keys and Missy Elliott, and the live album Live at Wembley (2004), filmed from her performance at Wembley Arena in London. She also premiered songs during her first solo concert on June 14, 2003, and promoted the album on television shows such as Saturday Night Live, Late Show with David Letterman, Today, The Early Show, and The View. The album's creative process was shaped by Beyoncé's desire to grow as an artist, with her selecting producers through meetings and sending song drafts to potential collaborators, including Jay-Z, Sean Paul, and Missy Elliott. Some tracks, like "Wrapped Around Me" with Elliott and Timbaland, were not included, and P. Diddy contributed to "Summertime," which was later sent to radio stations. With 43 songs completed, Beyoncé is credited as a co-writer, co-producer, and executive producer alongside her father and manager Mathew Knowles. The album's diverse instrumentation and genre influences, including hip-hop from Jay-Z, Outkast, and Lil' Kim, reggae from Sean Paul, and Arabic music from Scott Storch, reflect its broad musical range. Beyoncé stated that the album was lyrically similar to Destiny's Child's work but allowed her to write more personal, emotionally deep songs. While the album's content is not directly tied to her personal experiences, it explores universal themes of love, and she emphasized that love is something everyone experiences. Despite rumors of her relationship with Jay-Z, she remained silent, stating that music allows for interpretation and personal boundaries. A pre-order offer included a download of "I Can't Take No More," and the album's release was preceded by a promotional concert broadcast in over 20 U.S. theaters. The album's success was further supported by the strong performance of "Crazy in Love," which topped the Billboard Hot 100 and remained at number one for eight weeks, becoming Beyoncé's first number-one single as a solo artist.

Beyoncé's debut solo album, Dangerously in Love, was filmed for her live album Live at Wembley, released on April 26, 2004. In April 2003, Columbia Records selected between two songs for the lead single from the album by sending them to clubs; "Crazy in Love" was ultimately released as the lead single on May 14, 2003. Critics praised it as "deliriously catchy," and it topped the US Billboard Hot 100 based on heavy rotation, spending eight consecutive weeks at number one, becoming Beyoncé's first solo number-one single. The same week, Dangerously in Love reached number one on the Billboard 200. According to Nielsen SoundScan, "Crazy in Love" was the most downloaded song in the United States for four consecutive weeks in July 2003 and was certified sextuple platinum by the RIAA. The song achieved chart success internationally, reaching number one in Croatia, Ireland, and the United Kingdom. At the 46th Annual Grammy Awards in 2004, it won Best R&B Song and Best Rap/Sung Collaboration. The Jake Nava-directed music video, which portrays a woman embracing love and doing things she normally wouldn't, was critically acclaimed and won Best Female Video, Best R&B Video, and Best Choreography at the 2003 MTV Video Music Awards. "Baby Boy," released as the second single on August 3, 2003, was praised as a "high-profile collaboration" bridging R&B and dancehall, peaking at number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 eight weeks after its debut and staying there for nine consecutive weeks, surpassing "Crazy in Love" in duration. It was certified platinum by the RIAA and reached number two on the UK Singles Chart, topping the top ten in 15 other countries. The video, also directed by Nava, features Beyoncé performing with heavy choreography at a flooded party and on a Miami beach. "Me, Myself and I," released on October 19, 2003, received positive critical response for its production and vocal performance, peaking at number four on the US Billboard Hot 100 and reaching the top ten in Canada. It was certified platinum by the RIAA and reached the top 20 in Australia, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. The Johan Renck-directed music video shows events of Beyoncé dealing with an adulterous boyfriend in reverse and was nominated for Best R&B Video at the 2004 MTV Video Music Awards. "Naughty Girl," released on March 14, 2004, was lauded for borrowing elements from Donna Summer's "Love to Love You Baby" and peaked at number three on the US Billboard Hot 100, continuing Beyoncé's string of top-five singles. It was certified platinum by the RIAA and became a top-ten hit in Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. Despite not reaching number one, "Me, Myself and I" and "Naughty Girl" contributed to the album achieving multi-platinum status. The Nava-directed music video for "Naughty Girl" features Beyoncé seductively dancing and flirting with Usher in a Studio 54-styled setting inspired by Cyd Charisse and Fred Astaire in The Band Wagon and won Best Female Video at the 2004 MTV Video Music Awards. A promotional single, "Daddy," was released via iTunes on June 3, 2003, and Beyoncé and Luther Vandross's cover of "The Closer I Get to You" was released on June 13, 2004 as the final single from Vandross's album Dance with My Father. The Vandross cover won Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals at the 46th Annual Grammy Awards and peaked at number 62 on the US Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs. "Dangerously in Love 2," though not released as a single, won Best Female R&B Vocal Performance at the 46th Annual Grammy Awards and peaked at number 57 on the US Billboard Hot 100, with its master tone certified gold by the RIAA. Dangerously in Love received generally favorable reviews with a Metacritic score of 63 based on 17 reviews. Anthony DeCurtis of Rolling Stone noted the album presents Beyoncé in two styles, with ballads being less flattering, and Neil Drumming of Entertainment Weekly praised Beyoncé's innovation and range, though both noted missteps in the latter part. Sal Cinquemani of Slant Magazine highlighted Beyoncé's vocal experimentation and coquettish persona, Steve Jones of USA Today noted her greater depth as a songwriter and broader range as a singer, Ben Ratliff of Blender praised her performance and vocal arrangements, and Mark Anthony Neal of PopMatters called it an "artistic leap" and described it as Beyoncé at the peak of her womanhood. Uncut criticized the ballads as "self-pitying/self-mythologising," and Q stated she had good songs but no great ones. Natalie Nichols of the Los Angeles Times noted vocal finesse but criticized the ballads for being overlong. Jason King of Vibe said the album sometimes "sounds desperate to reach every demographic," Kelefa Sanneh of The New York Times felt it missed the harmonies of Destiny's Child, Rob Fitzpatrick of NME called it "a cruel glimpse of a talent that occasionally blazes but is frustratingly inconsistent," and Adam Sweeting of The Guardian wrote that the album lacked distinctive identity. Robert Christgau gave the album a one-star honorable mention, citing "Yes" and "Baby Boy" as highlights and quipping that the artist was "Dangerously in Love ... with her daddy," and noted it was a worthy effort for those attuned to its aesthetic. Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic stated the first half is strong enough to make it one of the best mainstream urban R&B records of 2003 and suggested Beyoncé might be better off pursuing a solo career. The album and its singles earned Beyoncé numerous awards and nominations, including New Female Artist and New R&B Artist at the 2003 Billboard Music Awards, a nomination for Favorite Soul/R&B Album at the 2003 American Music Awards, a nomination for Best Album at the 2003 MOBO Awards, and Best Contemporary R&B Album at the 46th Annual Grammy Awards, where she tied with Alicia Keys, Norah Jones, and Lauryn Hill for most Grammy Awards won by a female artist in one night. At the 2004 Brit Awards, the album was nominated for Best International Album but lost to Justin Timberlake's Justified, while Beyoncé won International Female Solo Artist. It was also nominated for Best Album at the 2004 MTV Europe Music Awards. In the United States, Dangerously in Love debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 on July 12, 2003, with first-week sales of 317,000 copies according to Nielsen SoundScan, making it the highest first-week sales among Destiny's Child members' solo albums. Although it fell short of Survivor's 663,000 first-week sales, it surpassed Kelly Rowland's Simply Deep and Michelle Williams' Heart to Yours. Beyoncé became the first female artist and the fifth artist ever to simultaneously top both the singles and albums charts in the United States and the United Kingdom, following the Beatles, Simon & Garfunkel, Rod Stewart, and Men at Work. In its second week, sales dropped 42% to 183,000 copies, placing it at number two behind Ashanti's Chapter II, and it remained at number two in its third week with 132,000 copies sold. The album is certified sextuple platinum by the RIAA and remains Beyoncé's best-selling album in the United States to date, with cumulative sales of over five million copies as of December 2015. In Canada, it debuted at number one on the Canadian Albums Chart and is certified triple platinum by Music Canada. Across Europe, it reached number one in Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, and Norway and topped the European Top 100 Albums. It was certified platinum by the IFPI in November 2003 for one million copies sold in Europe. By July 2011, it had sold over 1,143,000 copies in the UK and was certified quadruple platinum by the BPI. In Australia, it debuted at number three and peaked at number two, later being certified triple platinum by ARIA. In New Zealand, it debuted at number 14 and peaked at number eight, later certified platinum by RIANZ. In Japan, it peaked at number 12 on the Oricon Albums Chart and was certified gold by the RIAJ. As of 2011, the album has sold over 11 million copies worldwide. The success of Dangerously in Love and its singles established Beyoncé as a viable solo artist, with Rebecca Louie of the New York Daily News calling her a "sultry solo star" who "blossomed from a girly group" and noted her rise as one of the most marketable artists. She appeared on numerous magazine covers, guested on television shows, and signed lucrative commercial deals, including a contract with PepsiCo in 2003 for television commercials. The album's success led the public to believe Destiny's Child was disbanding, though Beyoncé stated their side projects were only a brief diversion. Due to time constraints, Beyoncé put her solo aspirations on hold to focus on her Super Bowl XXXVIII performance, where she sang the US national anthem, and was busy recording Destiny's Child's fifth studio album, Destiny Fulfilled (2004), which became their final album and led to the group's disbandment in 2006. Following the disbandment, Beyoncé recorded her second solo studio album, B'Day (2006), which debuted at number one on the US Billboard 200 with first-week sales of 541,000 units, exceeding those of Dangerously in Love. Keith Caulfield of Billboard noted the album's "handsome debut" was due to goodwill from the success of her first album.
